 Are Americans Really Protecting Their Skin From The Sun?
 November 4, 2026 
 by Anna Zucker 
 WASHINGTON — Skin care can involve plenty of decisions before you even leave the house. There are moisturizers, serums, and treatments promising to help with dryness, wrinkles, or dark spots. Finding a routine that works can take time.
 Sun protection belongs in that daily conversation, too. Recent survey findings explored how Americans approach sunscreen, tanning, and the advice they encounter online. Here is what the research reveals about the habits shaping skin health.
 Survey Findings Reveal Gaps In Sunscreen Use
 How often does sunscreen make it into Americans’ skin care routines? A new review by Silver Mirror Facial Bar examined American Academy of Dermatology surveys on sunscreen use, sun exposure, and skin care habits. The goal was to explore how interest in protecting skin translates into everyday behavior.
 Here are some of the findings .
 Key Findings
 Regular Use Remains Uneven: In the 2026 survey , 57% of adults reported using sunscreen regularly, while 43% did not use it regularly.
 Sunburn Is Common: One-third said they had experienced a sunburn in the previous year.
 Skin Care Spending And Habits Differ: A 2025 survey found 73% used products or procedures to prevent premature aging, while 56% used sunscreen regularly.
 Cloudy Days Get Overlooked: Only 20% reported using sunscreen on cloudy days in the 2025 findings.
 Online Advice Has Influence: In 2026, 21% said they relied on Instagram or TikTok influencers for skin care advice.
 Concern About Aging Meets Inconsistent Protection
 Wrinkles and dark spots concern many Americans. In the 2025 aging and sunscreen release , half of adults worried about premature skin aging, yet 21% did not know sunscreen helps prevent it. Forty-three percent of adults report wrinkles or dark spots they believed came from sun exposure. 
 Ultraviolet radiation from the sun can damage skin, contributing to premature aging and increasing skin cancer risk. That damage can accumulate over time, making consistent protection important even before visible changes appear.
 The survey figures describe different habits across respondents, but do not establish that everyone using anti-aging products was skipping sunscreen.
 Social Media And Tanning Myths
 The 2026 findings also examined where people get their information. Among Gen Z adults ages 18–29, 36% named Instagram or TikTok influencers as their primary source of skin care advice.
 Nearly half of Americans reported encountering sunscreen misinformation online. More than 16 million adults reported they reduced or stopped using sunscreen due to claims they saw online, according to the AAD’s population estimate.
 Tanning misconceptions were also common. Twenty-nine percent believed tanning was safe if they avoided burning, while 19% believed a base tan could prevent sunburn or reduce cancer risk.
 A tan signals UV damage, according to the AAD. Avoiding a burn does not make tanning safe.
 An April 2025 release found 67% reported getting tanned or darker skin in 2024, and 35% reported sunburn.
 Building Sun Protection Into The Day
 The AAD recommends broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher on skin uncovered by clothing. Broad-spectrum protection covers both UVA and UVB rays.
 Apply it to exposed areas, including the ears, neck, and hands. When outdoors, reapply every two hours or immediately after swimming or sweating.
 Clouds do not block all UV rays. Shade, a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses, and sun-protective clothing provide additional protection.
 Methodology
 Silver Mirror reviewed and published the AAD findings. Versta Research surveyed 1,132 U.S. adults online from Jan. 19 to Feb. 2, 2026. Sampling accounted for demographic characteristics, and results were weighted to Census population estimates.
 The April 2025 release described a survey of 1,140 adults conducted Jan. 20 to Feb. 5, 2025. Both reported maximum margins of error of approximately three percentage points, assuming no sample bias.
 The findings rely on self-reports. Separate survey waves do not track the same individuals, and the change from 56% to 57% does not establish a trend. The data also do not show whether respondents who skipped regular sunscreen were the ones reporting sunburn.
 Make Room For Sun Protection
 A skin care routine can address several concerns at once. Sunscreen, shade, and protective clothing help reduce exposure that contributes to future damage. Making those habits part of an ordinary day gives skin protection a regular place alongside the products already on the bathroom shelf.
